fragments.text: Ladies and gentlemen, it's an honor to address you at the 6th Artificial Intelligence for Information Accessibility Conference held in commemoration of the International Day for Universal Access to Information Organized by UNESCO. Today, I'm pleased to share with you my lecture on title Artificial Intelligence at the Service of Humanity. As we know, we're living in new contexts. We live in a time defined by exponential era. Here in Mexico, more than 100 million people are Internet users, representing the 80% of the population. In Latin America, the figure is around 81%. And there is another revalent fact. 59% of the users are already interacting with artificial intelligence tools. AI is not an accessory. It has become a community of cognitive, creative and analytical tools, what some authors describe

as hybrid objects. Above all, AI acts as a sociocultural and symbolic mediator, deeply tied to language, serving as a bridge in communication and in the construction of meaning. Yet, in this new context, we must also recognize that in its integration, AI adopts human roles and epistemic virtues, like objectivity, responsibility, plausibility, reliability of knowledge and decision-making. The risk here lies in assigning to machine the profile as a scientific expert, capable of collecting, analyzing and standardizing data, without properly questioning the limit and basis. This is the framework of algorithmic collaboration between humans and machine, an interaction that, when properly oriented, amplifies our cognitive, analytical and creative capabilities. That, when poorly directed, can reinforce injustice and asymmetries.

In this landscape, AI has become a copilot that imitates human intelligence and multiplies productivity. We know and we now have systems of machine learning, narrow AI, specialized in specific domains. All AI as firing to match human cognition and future scenarios of superintelligence. All of these are reflected in daily application, like virtual assistance, voice and facial recognition, natural language processing, emotional analyze, automating recent generation of image, sounds and code. Modern interactions, audience segmentation or content creation. Generative AI, in particular, is redefining the way we produce and share information, but it also raises critical question, like, how do we face algorithmic gaps and injustice? How do we prevent AI from amplifying inequities, inequalities, polarization or misinformation?

AI is not only a driver of productivity and international cooperation, but also is a feel of geopolitical, cultural and ethical disputes. We must never forget that every algorithm carries social implications, like from Russia, racial and gender basis, to the way it malls collective imaginaries, redefineness, rationality around efficiency, effaciently and profits, or even generates artificial identities and aesthetics. In this sense, AI is not neutral. It is an active agent of symbolic mediation. Against this risk, it is essential to imagine and implement AI as a tool for the common good. First, let us consider epistemic justice. The possibility that AI facilitates more equitable access to knowledge, incorporating indigenous, female, rural and non-western ways of knowing.

Imagine system training on multicultural and multilingual corpora, with the colonial awareness that help overcome the marginalization of historically silenced voices. Second, the idea of integral ecology are planet as a common home. AI can help monitor ecosystems, anticipate climate crisis, optimize energy networks and promote sustainable public policies, always with a sense of intergenerational responsibility. A third dimension is the reconfiguration of the social, emotional, imaginary. AI generates narratives, emotions, and means that shape collective, effective culture. Here the ethical question becomes excessive. What kinds of emotions does AI reproduce? Are they ethnically acceptable? Can we demand frameworks to guide their production responsibly? AI also opens opportunities in public health, clinical, diagnosed, digital mental health,

conversational therapies, surgical assistant, and drug design. But this requires a bioethical approach to algorithms, grounded in the principle of known maleficence and justice, to avoid reproducing biomedical bases. Furthermore, AI can contribute to building a culture of peace, anticipating hate-speak, detecting polarization, fostering restorative justice, and generating intercultural narratives of dialogue. And even more, AI can strengthen public philosophy and democracy by detecting misinformation, analyzing public policies in real time, and amplifying the citizens' right to truth. Laterally, let us think of algorithmic aesthetics, new digital poetics where art and mission. Not to replace human creativity, but to expand and give a new meaning of context of exclusions. For AI to truly serve humanity, we must develop new competencies.

The first is critical and sustainable digital literacy. Citizens must be equipped to read algorithms critically, to understand their environmental footprint, and to question the values embedded in technological design. The second is the adaptability and continuous learning. The speed of change requires to constantly learn, crossing disciplinary boundaries and integrating technological, ethical, communicative, and humanistic knowledge. The third is the rehumanization of the digital bound. We must never forget that behind every data set and every interface, there are people with dignity, histories, and context deserving of respect. Boiled in these competencies means fostering responsibility and responsible social-technical imagination. Care for oneself and other, on AI's limits and the promotion of an active algorithm citizenship.

This implies overcoming knowledge fragmentation by articulating scientific, technical, and humanistic perspective. All of this plays before us enormous ethical and anthropological changes. AI confronts us with fundamental rights, the rights to truth, to identity, to privacy, to equality and non-discrimination, to cultural access, and to personal data protection. It also requires us to protect the most vulnerable people with disabilities, older adults, and marginalized communities, and topologically, the challenge is to resist the humanization, and remain faithful to ourselves and to our communities, to foster cultures of hope and sharing, and to sustain genuine encounters with the others. In short, ethics must guide the technological development, AI cannot be an end in itself.

It must be oriented by responsibility, dignity, and the common good. Maybe then, we'll be able to protect professions such as education, face the dangers of disinformation and ensure that our official intelligence truly become a resource at the service of humanity. I would like to conclude by repeating the question that gives meaning to this reflection. How can we ensure that our official intelligence is truly and truly at the service of the humanity? The answer requires fair regulation, ethical design, critical literacy, international cooperation, and above all, a humanistic vision that plays the person their dignity and the right to truth at the very center of everything. Thank you very much.
